questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That it was far away geographically and culturally. I wanted to live a daily life in a setting I was not used to back home.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was hard in the start to find a good rhythm in the daily life, but once I figured that out, it opened the door to many new experiences and things to do. There are of course so many things to do, and I only did a handful of them. It would probably take take a whole life to all the things you want to do, and that probably would not be enough either. I am happy with the things I managed to do, but I also want to go back for more experiences some day.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. We got all the necessary information by mail, and although there were lots of mails to read through, it was pretty straight forward to know all the essential things to do. There was also a good website from the university which guided one through the whole procedure from start to finish.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't receive any special assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was just through the host university, so it was a fairly straight forward procedure.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Don't trust what the university says the commute time is. Search on google maps, that is more reliable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a bit hard to know exactly which courses we could take, but the procedure of registering itself was easy.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We had sort of 2 catalogues that showed the same courses. I used the public catalogue to find the courses I wanted to take and then found them again in the registration website. It was important to make sure that you picked the same courses, as some of them was called the same but had different course codes depending on whether you were undergrad or master's student. One of the courses I took I found on a flyer we got handed at the introduction, this was for courses specifically designed for exchange student. These courses also showed up in the public catalogue, but I would not have been made aware of them, if not for the flyer.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I think we could always write them an email, but I didn't need help so I'm not exactly sure.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful. There were room for anyone who wanted to join the classes I wanted. There was one course I wanted to take that I couldn't because it wasn't allowed for exchange students to take that course.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do a proper search of which courses are available and what level they are on. I sometimes had to search other faculties than my main faculty, because some courses that was about something within my field was distributed by another faculty.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Technically I didn't take any Master level courses. But some of the courses I took had one course code for undergrad, and one course code for masters, and I was connected to the undergrad course code. So the level of the course could be argued to be on master level, even though it technically was a bachelor course for me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I think that it's very hard to top the quality of the teaching at UCPH. Some of the lecturers were very good at teaching the subject matter in a cohesive and clear way, but there were also some whose explanations were hard to follow.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Nuclear Physics, Particle Physics and Women In Science were definitely the courses that fit my level and abilities as a new 3rd year bachelor student the best. And they also fit my interests the best. I think Universal Biology, Topics In Information Science and Modern Physics and Machine Learning are also good courses if you are very interested in those subjects, but they were a bit harder I feel like.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Football, baseball, Japanese kanji writing etc. I don't know how many or what they could be as I didn't partake in any, but there were definitely a bunch.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Taking the trains, it is a joy. The public transport system is so good, especially in Tokyo, and local transportation is really cheap.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Chiba prefecture, Nikko, Hiroshima, various sightseeing places in Tokyo, for example: Tokyo Tower, Ueno Park, Eastern Gardens and so on.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, I like the local culture a lot, people were very friendly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: They are pretty shy towards foreign student a lot of the time if they can't speak English well. Some who can speak English are pretty out going and are looking for people to speak to, so those opportunities are definitely there.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Well, with the toilets you just have to press the button to spray water in your butt and get it over with as soon as you can, because it opens up new worlds of sitting at the toilet. It is definitely not something to be scared of. I didn't really think the differences were challenging as those differences was something I wanted to explore and seek out, so I was very open minded from the start. I think maybe the most challenging part was their very binary gender world view.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The people are kind and generous and helpful. People don't push each other on the metro and people were thoughtful of each other. It was like living in a giant bee hive where everybody did their part but still saw themselves, but importantly also each other, as individuals. Whereas in western society we only see ourselves as individuals, and always put our priorities before others.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Housing: There are two main choices when it comes to the housing provided by UTokyo: Mejirodai International Village (MIV) and Komaba Lodge (KL). The commute to Hongo campus is only 10 min faster by living at MIV, but the commute to Komaba campus is much faster by living at KL, as KL is right next to this campus. So it depends on which campus you are mostly going to be at, which means that you need to take a look at courses beforehand. Another thing is that MIV is clean, new and has good facilities and a good common area but it feels a bit like a prison sometimes, there are cameras everywhere, you are not allowed guests inside your room or on your floor, it is split up into binary genders and you have to have your keys with you to go to the toilet. Whereas KL is a bit dirty and old, but people are allowed to visit each other and I get the feeling that it's more open, it is also close to Shibuya if one like to party. I lived at MIV and I was happy living there, but I would also have been happy living at KL for other reasons. There are pros and cons of both places, so it's up to you to weigh them according to your needs.

Lunch: You can become a member of Coop for a fee. Then you can get lunch for 20% off. The thing is, you get the fee back at the end if you remember to go to the office, so it's basicly free 20% off in the cafeterias and Coop shop if you have the membership.

Local transportation: Depending on how many days of the week you are going to a campus, you can maybe make it cheaper for yourself if you get a transportation pass thing. I didn't get it because it was not worth it for me. Also: Get a PASMO card in the airport as you arrive, you need at least 2000 yen to get it, and it will be much easier in the long run to have it rather than buying tickets, so you might as well get it as the first thing when you arrive.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are 2 main cafeterias at Hongo campus: one is just in front and underground of the Yasuta auditorium, this is the largest cafeteria and has a bit more dishes than the second one, but you are underground. The other one is located right next to the bus stop and science buildings, in the same building as the Coop office thing. This cafeteria has windows and is less crowded at lunch time, so this was my favourite place to eat lunch. If you have classes both at Hongo and at Komaba I would recommend living at Komaba Lodge instead of MIV. But if you live at MIV, Ikebukuro and Iidabashi are pretty close by, only 2 metro stops in either direction on the Yurakucho line, and here there are a lot of places to get food and other things. If you want used books, CD's, LP's or Pokemon cards, go to BookOff, it is a really nice store with a lot of locations around Tokyo. I got a fairly rare CD from one of them for pretty cheap. There are also some pretty cool train lines at the harbour area that I can recommend to take. Also, if you arrive at Haneda Airport, I would highly recommend to take the Tokyo Monorail instead of the other train.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living a daily life in Tokyo.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Overcoming home sickness the first month, but it gets a lot better when starting courses and meeting a bunch of people.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
